objectives.title: Master setInputFiles(), download handling, and file validation

Easy.q: How do you bypass the OS dialog and upload the file natively using Playwright?
options: Use `page.keyboard.type('path/to/file.pdf')`.
Use the `locator.setInputFiles('path/to/file.pdf')` method directly on the `<input type="file">` element.
Drag and drop the file via the mouse API.
Upload the file to an AWS S3 bucket and pass the URL.
Easy.a: Use the `locator.setInputFiles('path/to/file.pdf')` method directly on the `<input type="file">` element.
Easy.explanation: Native file inputs (`<input type="file">`) intercept operating system file dialogs. Playwright bypasses the OS dialog completely. `setInputFiles` mathematically injects the file buffer directly into the browser's memory, simulating an instant, flawless upload.
Easy.scenario: You are testing an avatar upload feature. Clicking the 'Upload' button opens the native OS Windows file dialog, which Playwright cannot interact with.

Easy.q: What is the specific architectural purpose of passing an empty array `[]` to `setInputFiles`?
options: It crashes the test.
It clears the file input. If a file was previously selected, passing an empty array instantly removes it from the input element's internal buffer.
It uploads a zero-byte file.
It opens the OS file picker.
Easy.a: It clears the file input. If a file was previously selected, passing an empty array instantly removes it from the input element's internal buffer.
Easy.explanation: Just like `fill('')` clears a text box, passing an empty array is the API standard for clearing the internal file `FileList` array of a native HTML input.

Easy.scenario: You click a 'Download Invoice' button, and a PDF file begins downloading to your local machine.
Easy.q: How do you mathematically instruct Playwright to wait for the download to finish and capture the resulting file object?
options: Wait 10 seconds, then check the `C:/Downloads` folder.
Use `const download = await page.waitForEvent('download');`
Use `await page.click('button', { download: true });`
Use `const pdf = await page.getByRole('button').download();`
Easy.a: Use `const download = await page.waitForEvent('download');`
Easy.explanation: Downloads in modern browsers are asynchronous streams. You must listen for the specific `download` event emitted by the `Page` object. This event yields a `Download` object that provides access to the file's path, filename, and completion status.

Easy.scenario: You have successfully captured a `Download` object.
Easy.q: Which of the following actions can you perform on this object? (Select all that apply)
options: await download.path() // Get the temporary path on disk.
await download.saveAs('/reports/invoice.pdf') // Save a permanent copy.
await download.cancel() // Abort the download mid-stream.
await download.click() // Open the file in the browser.
a: await download.path() // Get the temporary path on disk.
await download.saveAs('/reports/invoice.pdf') // Save a permanent copy.
await download.cancel() // Abort the download mid-stream.
Easy.explanation: The `Download` object is incredibly powerful. Because Playwright saves downloads to a volatile temporary folder (which is deleted when the browser closes), `saveAs` is the standard method for persisting the file to a permanent location for validation.

Easy.scenario: A form requires you to upload 3 photos simultaneously.
Easy.q: How do you upload multiple files using `setInputFiles`?
options: Call `setInputFiles` three separate times.
You must zip the files.
Pass an array of file paths: `await input.setInputFiles(['img1.jpg', 'img2.jpg', 'img3.jpg'])`.
Multiple files cannot be uploaded via automation.
Easy.a: Pass an array of file paths: `await input.setInputFiles(['img1.jpg', 'img2.jpg', 'img3.jpg'])`.
Easy.explanation: If the HTML input has the `multiple` attribute, Playwright accepts an array of strings. It injects all files into the `FileList` object simultaneously.

Medium.q: Why is the `Promise.all` Trigger Pattern absolutely mandatory for handling downloads, rather than writing them sequentially on separate lines?
options: It improves speed.

If you write them sequentially, the click action fires the download event. If the download is fast (e.g., a small CSV), the event fires and resolves *before* Node.js reaches the next line to execute `waitForEvent`. The test will then hang infinitely waiting for an event that already happened.
It is just a stylistic preference.
It prevents the file from saving to disk.
Medium.a: If you write them sequentially, the click action fires the download event. If the download is fast (e.g., a small CSV), the event fires and resolves *before* Node.js reaches the next line to execute `waitForEvent`. The test will then hang infinitely waiting for an event that already happened.
Medium.explanation: This is the most critical concurrency concept in Node.js automation. You must attach the listener (`waitForEvent`) *at the exact same millisecond* you trigger the action. `Promise.all` guarantees both promises are evaluated concurrently, eliminating the race condition.

Medium.scenario: You are testing an application that does not use a native `<input type="file">`. Instead, it uses a custom Javascript widget. When you click it, the OS File Explorer native dialog pops up.
Medium.q: Because Playwright cannot interact with the Windows/Mac OS native UI, how do you handle this? (Select all that apply)
options: Use `const [fileChooser] = await Promise.all([page.waitForEvent('filechooser'), page.click('.custom-upload-btn')]);`
You must use a third-party library like RobotJS.
Once the `fileChooser` is intercepted, use `await fileChooser.setFiles('path/to/file.jpg');`.
Playwright cannot automate this scenario.
a: Use `const [fileChooser] = await Promise.all([page.waitForEvent('filechooser'), page.click('.custom-upload-btn')]);`
Once the `fileChooser` is intercepted, use `await fileChooser.setFiles('path/to/file.jpg');`.
Medium.explanation: This is Playwright's genius architecture. It intercepts the browser's request to the Operating System to open the file dialog. It captures that request as a `filechooser` event, suppressing the OS popup completely, and allows you to programmatically inject the files via `fileChooser.setFiles()`.

Medium.scenario: You are running tests in headless CI. You trigger a download and try to read it using `await download.path()`. The test crashes randomly.
Medium.q: What environmental configuration is necessary to ensure downloads work reliably in CI?
options: You must configure a custom `downloadsPath` in your Playwright config.
You must install Chrome instead of using the Playwright binaries.
Downloads are enabled by default. The issue is likely that the test finishes and closes the browser context before the download stream has finished saving the bytes to disk.
You must run in headed mode.
Medium.a: Downloads are enabled by default. The issue is likely that the test finishes and closes the browser context before the download stream has finished saving the bytes to disk.
Medium.explanation: By default, Playwright accepts all downloads and streams them to a temporary directory. `await download.path()` inherently waits for the file to finish writing. However, if you don't await the path, or if you close the `page` context immediately after the trigger, the temporary files are instantly deleted.

Medium.q: What architectural capability does this specific object payload unlock?
options: It bypasses virus scanning.
It allows you to upload a file entirely from memory without it ever existing on the physical hard drive. This is crucial for generating dynamic, on-the-fly test data.
It encrypts the file.
It uploads the file synchronously.
Medium.a: It allows you to upload a file entirely from memory without it ever existing on the physical hard drive. This is crucial for generating dynamic, on-the-fly test data.
Medium.explanation: In enterprise CI, managing hundreds of static dummy files (PDFs, images) is a nightmare. Playwright allows you to pass a Buffer object. You can dynamically generate a 5MB text file or CSV in Node.js memory and upload it instantly without touching the file system.

Medium.scenario: You click 'Download CSV', but the application does not trigger a native browser download. Instead, it opens a new tab containing the raw comma-separated text.
Medium.q: Because the `download` event is never fired, how must you architecturally capture this data?
options: It is impossible.
Use the `waitForEvent('popup')` pattern to capture the new `Page` object, wait for it to load, and then use `await newPage.content()` or `locator.innerText()` to extract the raw text.
Use `page.on('request')`.
Use `setInputFiles()`.
Medium.a: Use the `waitForEvent('popup')` pattern to capture the new `Page` object, wait for it to load, and then use `await newPage.content()` or `locator.innerText()` to extract the raw text.
Medium.explanation: Not all 'downloads' are downloads. If the server responds with an inline disposition (e.g., `Content-Disposition: inline`) or simply returns text, the browser renders it rather than downloading it. You must switch paradigms and treat the 'download' as a new window interaction.

Hard.code:
const response = await page.waitForResponse(res => res.url().includes('/api/upload') && res.status() === 200);
expect(response.ok()).toBeTruthy();
Hard.q: A Junior SDET is using `setInputFiles()`, but the test is flaky because sometimes the next assertion fires before the server has processed the file. How does this code snippet provide absolute, architectural stability to the upload flow?
options: It checks if the server is online.

It synchronizes the frontend test execution with the backend network layer. By explicitly waiting for the `200 OK` API response from the upload endpoint, the test absolutely guarantees the file is fully uploaded and processed before proceeding to the next UI interaction.
It pauses the test for 200 milliseconds.
It intercepts the payload and modifies it.
Hard.a: It synchronizes the frontend test execution with the backend network layer. By explicitly waiting for the `200 OK` API response from the upload endpoint, the test absolutely guarantees the file is fully uploaded and processed before proceeding to the next UI interaction.
Hard.explanation: UI testing is an illusion. Just because the progress bar says 100% does not mean the backend database has committed the file. Enterprise architects always bind critical UI flows (uploads, payments) to the underlying Network API responses to eliminate race conditions.

Hard.scenario: Your application uploads massive 500MB video files. Using `setInputFiles()` works, but it takes 60 seconds per test, drastically slowing down your CI pipeline.
Hard.q: What is the most robust, enterprise-grade architectural solution to test the UI's handling of a 500MB upload without actually spending 60 seconds uploading 500MB?
options: Increase the test timeout to 5 minutes.
Compress the video to a zip file.

Use `page.route()` to intercept the `POST /upload` API call. You can use `setInputFiles` with a tiny 1KB dummy file, intercept the network request, and instantly mock a `200 OK` success response. This allows you to test the UI success state in 10 milliseconds.
Disable file uploads in the test environment.
Hard.a: Use `page.route()` to intercept the `POST /upload` API call. You can use `setInputFiles` with a tiny 1KB dummy file, intercept the network request, and instantly mock a `200 OK` success response. This allows you to test the UI success state in 10 milliseconds.
Hard.explanation: E2E tests should not be load tests. If you are testing the UI logic (does the success modal appear?), you do not need to push half a gigabyte through the CI network. Mocking the API boundary allows you to surgically verify frontend logic at lightning speed.

Hard.scenario: You have captured a `Download` object. You want to verify that the downloaded PDF file actually contains the string `Invoice #999`.
Hard.q: What is the correct architectural sequence of Node.js operations required to achieve this? (Select all that apply)
options: Use `await download.saveAs('temp.pdf')` to persist the file.
Use Playwright's `expect(download).toHaveText('Invoice #999')`.
Use Node's native `fs.readFileSync('temp.pdf')` or a dedicated PDF parsing library (like `pdf-parse`) to extract the text buffer.
Write a standard JS string assertion: `expect(extractedText).toContain('Invoice #999')`.
a: Use `await download.saveAs('temp.pdf')` to persist the file.
Use Node's native `fs.readFileSync('temp.pdf')` or a dedicated PDF parsing library (like `pdf-parse`) to extract the text buffer.
Write a standard JS string assertion: `expect(extractedText).toContain('Invoice #999')`.
Hard.explanation: Playwright is a browser automation tool, not a file parser. It cannot read the internal binary contents of PDFs or Excel files. You must bridge Playwright with the Node.js ecosystem. Save the file, use a specialized Node library to parse the binary, and then assert on the output.

Hard.q: What is the extreme performance advantage of using `createReadStream()` instead of `saveAs()` when analyzing massive files (e.g., a 2GB CSV)?
options: There is no difference.

It allows Node.js to stream the bytes directly from the browser's memory into your assertion logic in chunks. You do not have to wait for the 2GB file to finish writing to disk, and you do not crash Node's V8 memory heap.
It automatically unzips the file.
It bypasses network security.
Hard.a: It allows Node.js to stream the bytes directly from the browser's memory into your assertion logic in chunks. You do not have to wait for the 2GB file to finish writing to disk, and you do not crash Node's V8 memory heap.
Hard.explanation: Enterprise applications deal with massive data. If you use `saveAs` and `readFileSync` on a 2GB file, Node.js will throw an Out Of Memory (OOM) error. Utilizing Node's native Stream API via `createReadStream` is the pinnacle of performance optimization.

Hard.scenario: A developer created a custom drag-and-drop zone (`<div class="dropzone">`) that does NOT contain an `<input type="file">`. `setInputFiles` and `filechooser` interception both fail.
Hard.q: How must you architecturally force a file upload into this custom drag-and-drop zone?
options: It is impossible.
You must use `page.evaluate()` to construct a synthetic `DataTransfer` object, attach your file buffer to it, and programmatically dispatch a `drop` Event directly onto the `.dropzone` DOM element.
Use `page.mouse.move()`.
Use `page.keyboard.press('Enter')`.
Hard.a: You must use `page.evaluate()` to construct a synthetic `DataTransfer` object, attach your file buffer to it, and programmatically dispatch a `drop` Event directly onto the `.dropzone` DOM element.
Hard.explanation: When developers bypass standard HTML APIs, standard automation APIs fail. To simulate a native OS drag-and-drop without OS access, you must drop into the browser console (`evaluate`), forge the internal Javascript payload (`DataTransfer`), and trigger the event manually. This is a very advanced workaround.

meta.outcome: Handle popups, new tabs, and multi-window workflows

objectives.title: Use popup events and multiple browser contexts

Easy.q: In Playwright, what is the architectural relationship between a 'Browser Context' and a 'Page'?
options: They are the same thing.
A Browser Context is an isolated incognito session (containing its own cookies and cache). A Page is a single tab or window inside that Context. One Context can contain multiple Pages.
A Page contains multiple Contexts.
A Context is the physical browser binary.
Easy.a: A Browser Context is an isolated incognito session (containing its own cookies and cache). A Page is a single tab or window inside that Context. One Context can contain multiple Pages.
Easy.explanation: Understanding this hierarchy is vital. When a user clicks a link that opens a new tab, that new tab is instantiated as a new `Page` object, but it shares the exact same `Context` (meaning it shares login cookies) as the original tab.

Easy.code: await page.getByText('Open Dashboard').click(); // Opens in new tab
Easy.q: If you immediately run `await page.locator('.dashboard-header').click()` after this line, what will happen?
options: It clicks the header on the new tab.

It crashes. The `page` variable is strictly bound to the original tab. Even though a new tab opened visually, Playwright does not automatically switch focus. It will search for `.dashboard-header` on the original tab and fail.
Playwright automatically switches `page` to the most recently opened tab.
It clicks both tabs.
Easy.a: It crashes. The `page` variable is strictly bound to the original tab. Even though a new tab opened visually, Playwright does not automatically switch focus. It will search for `.dashboard-header` on the original tab and fail.
Easy.explanation: Unlike human users, Playwright does not have a concept of 'active window focus'. Variables are immutable pointers. `page` points to Tab A. If Tab B opens, you must capture Tab B into a new variable (`const newPage`) to interact with it.

Easy.scenario: A link has the attribute `target="_blank"`, which forces the browser to open it in a new tab.
Easy.q: What is the standard Playwright syntax to explicitly wait for and capture this new tab?
options: const newPage = await page.waitForNavigation();
const [newPage] = await Promise.all([context.waitForEvent('page'), page.click('a[target="_blank"]')]);
const newPage = await context.newPage();
await page.switchTo().window();
Easy.a: const [newPage] = await Promise.all([context.waitForEvent('page'), page.click('a[target="_blank"]')]);
Easy.explanation: This is the classic Promise.all Trigger Pattern. You listen for the `page` event (which fires whenever a new tab/window is created) at the exact same time you click the link. The event yields the brand new `Page` object.

Easy.scenario: You have successfully captured `newPage` from a popup.
Easy.q: Which of the following statements are true regarding the two tabs? (Select all that apply)
options: You can interact with both concurrently: `await Promise.all([page.click('#btnA'), newPage.click('#btnB')])`.
You must close the original page before interacting with the new page.
They share the exact same cookies and `localStorage` because they belong to the same Browser Context.
You must call `switchTo()` whenever you want to change which page you are automating.
a: You can interact with both concurrently: `await Promise.all([page.click('#btnA'), newPage.click('#btnB')])`.
They share the exact same cookies and `localStorage` because they belong to the same Browser Context.
Easy.explanation: Because `page` and `newPage` are just independent Node.js object references, you can interact with them simultaneously. There is no `switchTo` overhead. This makes automating complex multi-window workflows incredibly fast.

Easy.scenario: Your test is finished interacting with `newPage`.
Easy.q: What is the best practice for handling the extra tab?
options: Leave it open; Playwright handles it.
Call `await newPage.close();` to free up system memory and keep the context clean.
Call `await context.close();`.
Call `await page.goBack();`.
Easy.a: Call `await newPage.close();` to free up system memory and keep the context clean.
Easy.explanation: While the entire context is destroyed at the end of the test, it is a best practice to close popup tabs immediately after verifying them to prevent memory leaks and rogue background network requests during the rest of the test.

Medium.q: What is the specific difference between `waitForEvent('popup')` and `waitForEvent('page')`?
options: There is no difference; they are aliases for the exact same underlying Context event. Playwright intercepts window creation via `window.open` or `target="_blank"`.
`popup` only fires for modal dialogs.
`page` only fires when you manually call `context.newPage()`.
`popup` captures iframes.
Medium.a: There is no difference; they are aliases for the exact same underlying Context event. Playwright intercepts window creation via `window.open` or `target="_blank"`.
Medium.explanation: Both events yield the exact same `Page` object. `popup` is tied specifically to the `Page` object emitting it (a child spawned from a parent), whereas `page` is emitted by the `BrowserContext`. Conceptually, they achieve the exact same goal in tab interception.

Medium.scenario: You are writing a test that opens 3 different tabs. You lose track of your variables.
Medium.q: How can you dynamically query the `BrowserContext` to find a specific tab based on its current URL? (Select all that apply)
options: const pages = context.pages();
const targetPage = pages.find(p => p.url().includes('dashboard'));
const targetPage = await context.waitForEvent('url');
const pages = await page.allTabs();
a: const pages = context.pages();
const targetPage = pages.find(p => p.url().includes('dashboard'));
Medium.explanation: `context.pages()` returns an array of all currently active `Page` objects within that session. You can iterate over this array and use standard JS `find` to dynamically locate a tab based on its URL or title, allowing self-healing multi-tab navigation.

Medium.scenario: A test requires you to log in as an 'Admin' and a 'User' simultaneously to test a live chat feature.
Medium.q: Because a single Browser Context shares cookies, if you log into Tab A as Admin, Tab B will also be Admin. How do you architecturally solve this in Playwright?
options: Use Incognito mode on the OS.
Clear the cookies in Tab B.
Instantiate two entirely separate `BrowserContext` objects. Create `adminPage` in Context A, and `userPage` in Context B. They will have mathematically isolated cookie jars.
It is impossible in a single test.
Medium.a: Instantiate two entirely separate `BrowserContext` objects. Create `adminPage` in Context A, and `userPage` in Context B. They will have mathematically isolated cookie jars.
Medium.explanation: This is a superpower of Playwright. You can spawn multiple `BrowserContext` instances within the exact same test file. This allows you to simulate multiple distinct users interacting with each other in real-time, all coordinated from a single Node.js script.

Medium.q: If the `#external-link` opens a heavy, slow-loading React application, do you need to manually add `await newPage.waitForLoadState('networkidle')` before the assertion?
options: Yes, otherwise the assertion will execute instantly on a blank page.
Yes, because new tabs do not inherit auto-waiting.

No. Playwright's Web-First Assertions (`toHaveTitle`, `toBeVisible`) automatically poll the DOM. Even if the new tab is blank for 3 seconds, `toHaveTitle` will continuously retry until the title matches or the 5-second timeout is reached.
No, because `waitForEvent` automatically waits for network idle.
Medium.a: No. Playwright's Web-First Assertions (`toHaveTitle`, `toBeVisible`) automatically poll the DOM. Even if the new tab is blank for 3 seconds, `toHaveTitle` will continuously retry until the title matches or the 5-second timeout is reached.
Medium.explanation: Playwright's architecture allows you to delete thousands of lines of `waitFor` logic. Once you capture the `newPage` pointer, you immediately write assertions against it. The assertion engine handles all the latency and rendering delays natively.

Medium.scenario: A legacy test suite tests an email workflow: It triggers a password reset, opens a new tab to a temporary email service (like Mailinator), extracts the code, closes the tab, and pastes it into the original tab.
Medium.q: While possible in Playwright, why do Enterprise Architects heavily discourage this multi-tab UI approach?
options: Because Playwright cannot interact with Mailinator.

Because UI-driven email testing is inherently flaky and slow. The architectural best practice is to trigger the reset via the UI, but retrieve the email code synchronously via a Backend API call to a service like Mailosaur, completely bypassing the need for a second tab.
Because tabs crash the CI server.
Because it causes Strict Mode violations.
Medium.a: Because UI-driven email testing is inherently flaky and slow. The architectural best practice is to trigger the reset via the UI, but retrieve the email code synchronously via a Backend API call to a service like Mailosaur, completely bypassing the need for a second tab.
Medium.explanation: Just because you *can* automate multiple tabs doesn't mean you *should*. The most robust UI tests minimize UI surface area. Querying APIs for external dependencies (emails, SMS) is exponentially faster and more reliable than driving a third-party UI.

Hard.q: A developer writes this global listener to automatically log the title of any popup that opens during a massive E2E flow. What severe architectural race condition does this create?
options: The `popup` object cannot be logged.

Unawaited floating Promises. The callback function is `async`, but `page.on` is a synchronous event emitter. Playwright fires the event, but Node.js does not `await` the callback. The test might finish and close the browser while `popup.waitForLoadState()` is still pending, causing fatal `Target Closed` exceptions.
It blocks the main thread.
It triggers strict mode.
Hard.a: Unawaited floating Promises. The callback function is `async`, but `page.on` is a synchronous event emitter. Playwright fires the event, but Node.js does not `await` the callback. The test might finish and close the browser while `popup.waitForLoadState()` is still pending, causing fatal `Target Closed` exceptions.
Hard.explanation: This is a critical Node.js concept. `EventEmitter.on()` does not return a Promise. If you do asynchronous work inside an event listener without a top-level await orchestrating it, you leak floating promises. This is a primary source of "random" CI crashes at the end of tests.

Hard.scenario: You click a button. The application uses JavaScript `window.open('/invoice', '_blank')` to open a popup, but it also heavily manipulates the DOM in the *original* tab simultaneously.
Hard.q: How do you architect a `Promise.all` that safely captures the popup AND ensures the original tab's DOM manipulation has completed?
options: You cannot do both.
const [popup] = await Promise.all([ page.waitForEvent('popup'), page.waitForResponse('/api/invoice-generated'), page.click('#generate') ]);
Use a `for` loop.
Use `page.waitForTimeout(5000)`.
Hard.a: const [popup] = await Promise.all([ page.waitForEvent('popup'), page.waitForResponse('/api/invoice-generated'), page.click('#generate') ]);
Hard.explanation: `Promise.all` can orchestrate unlimited concurrent listeners. By attaching a listener for the popup *and* a listener for the background API request on the main page, you create an absolute, deterministic synchronization point that guarantees both the foreground and background architectures have settled.

Hard.scenario: You need to verify an OAuth authentication flow (e.g., 'Log in with Google'). Clicking the button opens a popup to `accounts.google.com`. After login, the popup automatically closes, and the main page logs in.
Hard.q: What makes this architectural flow dangerous to automate using standard `popup` listeners? (Select all that apply)
options: Playwright cannot automate Google.
The popup might close itself before your Playwright code finishes interacting with it, resulting in `Target Closed` exceptions during `.fill()` commands.
Cross-origin popups are strictly blocked by the CDP.
You must race against the external application's redirect timers.
a: The popup might close itself before your Playwright code finishes interacting with it, resulting in `Target Closed` exceptions during `.fill()` commands.
You must race against the external application's redirect timers.
Hard.explanation: Automating 3rd-party OAuth popups is notoriously unstable because you do not control the external state machine. Google might redirect in 50ms or 500ms. If you are mid-assertion when the popup closes, the test crashes. The enterprise solution is often to mock the OAuth response via API.

Hard.code:
const newPage = await context.newPage();
await newPage.route('**/*', route => route.abort());
Hard.q: You spawn a new tab manually and apply a strict network interception route to it. Does this interception apply to the original `page` object?
options: Yes, because routes are applied at the BrowserContext level.

No. Routing applied to a specific `Page` object is strictly encapsulated to that page. The original page continues to process network requests normally. This allows you to simulate an offline state in Tab B while Tab A remains online.
Yes, because they share the same event loop.
No, routes only work on the first tab.
Hard.a: No. Routing applied to a specific `Page` object is strictly encapsulated to that page. The original page continues to process network requests normally. This allows you to simulate an offline state in Tab B while Tab A remains online.
Hard.explanation: This demonstrates the mathematical isolation of `Page` objects. Even within the same Context, `page.route()` provides surgical, tab-specific network modification. (Note: `context.route()` exists if you want global interception).

Hard.scenario: You are building a custom fixture that automatically intercepts any new tab opened during a test, injects a custom authentication token into its `localStorage`, and returns it.
Hard.q: Because `localStorage` is origin-specific, why must you wait for the new page to perform its initial navigation *before* injecting the token?
options: Because tokens are encrypted.

When `waitForEvent('page')` fires, the new `Page` object is instantly yielded at the `about:blank` URL. If you execute `page.evaluate()` to set `localStorage` immediately, you are setting it on `about:blank`. You must wait for the page to navigate to the target domain before injecting domain-specific storage.
Because `localStorage` is disabled in `about:blank`.
You cannot inject tokens into new tabs.
Hard.a: When `waitForEvent('page')` fires, the new `Page` object is instantly yielded at the `about:blank` URL. If you execute `page.evaluate()` to set `localStorage` immediately, you are setting it on `about:blank`. You must wait for the page to navigate to the target domain before injecting domain-specific storage.
Hard.explanation: This is a profound execution pipeline detail. The `page` event fires the millisecond the tab spawns, before the HTTP GET request is even sent. To manipulate the target application's state, you must await `waitForLoadState` or an explicit navigation, ensuring the JS context is anchored to the correct origin.
